name: New Testament
info: The New Testament is the second division of the Christian Bible: 27 texts in Koine Greek by various authors, including four gospels, Acts, letters and Revelation, mostly written in the mid to late first century and settled as a canon by the late fourth.

facts.made: Various authors, thought by scholars to be mostly Jewish Christians; the gospels are anonymous and carry names given by church tradition; thirteen letters present Paul the Apostle as their author
facts.form: A collection of 27 texts in Koine Greek: four gospels, the Acts of the Apostles, thirteen Pauline letters, Hebrews, seven Catholic epistles and the Book of Revelation
facts.where: Thousands of manuscripts: more than 5,800 in Greek, 10,000 in Latin and 9,300 in other ancient languages; Codex Vaticanus, Codex Sinaiticus and Codex Alexandrinus are among the earliest extant Christian Bibles
facts.known: The four gospels on the life, death and resurrection of Jesus; the letters of Paul; the Book of Revelation; the long process by which the canon formed; the thousands of manuscripts and their variants; translations from Syriac and Latin to Tyndale and the Authorized Version

t: The New Testament is a collection of 27 Christian texts in Koine Greek, made up of four gospels, Acts, epistles and Revelation, and forms the second division of the Christian Bible.
Its canon developed gradually over the first few centuries through debate, and Athanasius listed the 27 books in 367; scholars still disagree on the dates and authors of many of them.
It survives in thousands of manuscripts and translations, and textual criticism uses them to reconstruct the earliest recoverable text.
dyk: Irenaeus, writing around 180 CE, argued that there could be neither more nor fewer than four gospels, because there are four zones of the world and four principal winds.
ev: 1 Thessalonians, likely the earliest of Paul's letters, is written
Marcion draws up a canon of a modified version of Luke and ten of Paul's letters, and rejects the Old Testament
Irenaeus asserts that the four gospels are the only legitimate ones in Against Heresies
Eusebius lists the accepted, disputed and rejected writings in his Ecclesiastical History
Athanasius gives the list of the 27 books in his Easter letter and calls them canonized
The Council of Carthage accepts a summary of the lost acts of the Synod of Hippo Regius of 393
Martin Luther's translation of the New Testament appears
The Authorized Version, also called the King James Version, is published

sections.origins:
The New Testament is the second division of the Christian Bible. Together with the Old Testament, which is based primarily on the Hebrew Bible, it makes up the sacred scripture of Christianity. Its name rests on the idea of a new covenant that Christians believe completes or fulfils the covenant God made with Israel on Mount Sinai through Moses. Christians have traditionally found this new covenant foretold in the Book of Jeremiah; Judaism traditionally disagrees.

The word "testament" has a history of its own. The Hebrew word brit means 'alliance, covenant, pact'. The Jewish translators of the Septuagint, working in Alexandria in the 3rd and 2nd centuries BCE, rendered it with the Greek diathēkē, which in the Greek world usually meant a will left after a person's death. Scholars debate why they chose it. Christian theology has understood the choice to give the covenant something of the character of a will left by the death of Jesus.

The phrase as a name for a collection of Christian writings can be traced to Tertullian, who in Against Marcion, written c. 208 CE, spoke of the Divine Word as doubly edged "with the two testaments of the law and the gospel". By the 4th century an Old and a New Testament were established, though not yet their exact contents.
sections.content:
The New Testament is a collection of 27 Christian texts written in Koine Greek by various authors. Each of the four gospels narrates the life, death and resurrection of Jesus of Nazareth, although Mark in its original text ends with the empty tomb and has no account of appearances after the resurrection. "Gospel" comes from the Old English gōd-spell, "good news", which translates the Greek euangélion. Matthew, Mark and Luke are called the Synoptic Gospels because they share many stories, often in the same order and sometimes in the same words. John is quite different and begins with a philosophical prologue.

The Acts of the Apostles is a narrative of the apostles' ministry after the death and resurrection of Jesus, and functions as a sequel to the Gospel of Luke. Thirteen letters present Paul the Apostle as their author: nine to churches and four to individuals. Hebrews is anonymous. The Catholic epistles, a name meaning "general" or "universal", are James, 1 and 2 Peter, 1, 2 and 3 John, and Jude. The Book of Revelation, also called the Apocalypse of John, opens with letters to seven congregations of Asia Minor and then takes the form of an apocalypse, a "revealing" of divine prophecy.

The theologian Frank Stagg listed concerns common to its writers, among them that Jesus Christ is central and that his death and resurrection are at the heart of the whole event.
sections.making:
Literary analysis suggests that many of the texts were written in the mid to late first century. The earliest are the letters of Paul, and 1 Thessalonians is likely the earliest of them, written around 52 CE. There is no scholarly consensus on the date of the latest text. John A. T. Robinson, William F. Albright and others dated many or all of the books before 70 CE, while Bart D. Ehrman and Stephen L. Harris date some much later. Richard Pervo dated Luke–Acts to c. 115 CE.

The gospels are anonymous, as biographies of the time often were, and their names come from church tradition. Scholars hold that the names were fixed to them by the mid 2nd century. Most scholars hold to Marcan priority, the view that Mark was written first. Many argue that Matthew and Luke used Mark and a hypothetical Q source, though alternatives without Q are gaining ground. Most scholars understand the gospels as Greco-Roman biography. Seven letters of Paul are generally classed as undisputed: Romans, 1 and 2 Corinthians, Galatians, Philippians, 1 Thessalonians and Philemon. The authorship of six others is disputed, and most scholars regard the Pastoral epistles as pseudepigrapha.

It is generally agreed that the historical Jesus primarily spoke Aramaic, while the books were written in Koine Greek. Scholars differ on why its style departs from that of literary Greek of the period.
sections.reception:
The canon formed through a complex and lengthy process. Writings attributed to the apostles circulated among the earliest communities, and Paul's letters were circulating, perhaps in collected forms, by the end of the 1st century. Around 140 CE Marcion accepted only a version of Luke and ten of Paul's letters and rejected the Old Testament entirely; other Christians largely rejected his canon. Some scholars have argued that the church formulated its canon partly in response to him. In the mid 2nd century Justin Martyr mentioned "memoirs of the apostles" read on Sunday beside the "writings of the prophets". Irenaeus asserted a canon of four gospels around 180.

By the early 200s Origen may have been using the same 27 books, though Hebrews, James, 2 Peter, 2 and 3 John and Revelation were still disputed. Eusebius, c. 300, sorted writings into accepted, disputed and rejected. Athanasius's Easter letter of 367 listed the 27 books. The Synod of Hippo Regius (393), whose acts are lost, may have been the first council to accept the canon, and the Council of Carthage accepted a summary of its acts in 397 and 419. Lee Martin McDonald has written that the councils recognised books already prominent through use.
sections.survival:
Like other ancient literature, the text was preserved in manuscripts before printing. The earliest date from the late 2nd to early 3rd century, with the possible exception of Papyrus 52, whose early date has recently been called into question. Papyrus 90, 98 and 104 have also been thought to date as early as the 2nd century. The New Testament survives in more than 5,800 Greek manuscripts, 10,000 Latin manuscripts and 9,300 in other ancient languages, including Syriac, Slavic, Ethiopic and Armenian. Church writings also quote it so widely that the whole text could be assembled from them.

The manuscripts contain variants, almost all of them trivial matters of spelling, punctuation or grammar. The two most commonly cited of some importance are the last verses of the Gospel of Mark and the story of the woman taken in adultery in the Gospel of John. Many scholars regard the Johannine Comma in 1 John as a later addition. Bart D. Ehrman notes that scribal additions are often found in late medieval manuscripts but not in earlier ones.

Translations began at the end of the 2nd century, first into Syriac, Latin and Coptic. Renaissance humanists such as Lorenzo Valla and Erasmus urged a return to the original Greek, which began modern textual criticism.
sections.legacy:
The 16th century brought an explosion of vernacular translations: Martin Luther's (1522), William Tyndale's (1526) and the Authorized Version, or King James Version (1611). Later translations, among them the Revised Standard Version (1946), the New International Version (1973) and the English Standard Version (2001), have largely used critical editions of the Greek text as their base.

Christian churches hold the text in different ways. The Catholic Church teaches that divine revelation has one common source and two modes of transmission, Scripture and Tradition. Bishop Kallistos Ware says that for the Orthodox there is only one source, Holy Tradition, within which Scripture exists. Protestants, following sola scriptura, derive doctrine from scripture alone. Evangelicals hold it to be inerrant, as in the Chicago Statement on Biblical Inerrancy (1978), while Presbyterians generally do not insist on inerrancy. Latter-day Saints accept it "as far as it is translated correctly".

Most of its influence on the arts has come from the Gospels and Revelation. Earliest Christian art depicted the raising of Lazarus, the baptism of Jesus and the Good Shepherd. The Heliand and Passion plays followed in the Middle Ages, and the Passion has been a theme in film since La Passion (France, 1903).

summary: The New Testament is the second division of the Christian Bible, a collection of 27 Greek texts that includes four gospels, Acts, letters and Revelation. Its canon formed over several centuries, and it survives in thousands of manuscripts studied by textual critics.

notes: The article's dating section says 'There is scholarly consensus on the date of composition of the latest New Testament texts' while its lead says there is no consensus; I followed the lead and the section's own list of differing dates.
start 52 is 1 Thessalonians c. 52 CE, the article's earliest dated text; the oldest tradition behind the gospels is not dated.

The article says Revelation was not added till the Council of Carthage (419), yet also that the 397 council accepted the canon and Athanasius listed Revelation in 367; I left the Revelation claim out and give both Carthage dates only as the article does.
The article's remark that the Muratorian fragment is dated between 170 and the end of the 4th century is left out as too uncertain to place.
'21 epistles' is not in the article; the form fact lists the groups instead.

Left out: Geisler and Nix's 99.5% purity claim (advocacy, contested), the Messianic Judaism, Jehovah's Witnesses, Oneness Pentecostal and Adventist views for length, the claim about only educated elites writing the gospels, the Marcion/Luke-Acts authorship detail beyond the section's range.
